title: At 17, Navya Tuteja Built an AI Platform to Help Neurodivergent Job Seekers
excerpt: The Thomas Jefferson High School senior wrote the algorithm for Raaha herself — and did it at a school where ChatGPT and Claude are blocked on the Wi-Fi.
body:
• Navya Tuteja, 17, a senior at Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology in Virginia and president of its AI club, launched Raaha in 2026 — a free platform that helps neurodivergent job seekers score a listing for fit before applying. Within about two months it drew 1,000+ users and 20,000 job listings, according to Fortune.
  • Her school blocks ChatGPT and Claude on its Wi-Fi. Tuteja wrote Raaha's underlying algorithm herself, using AI only for routine tasks like website design — and argues bans miss the point: "I don't think banning it is the solution. I think you have to regulate it in the right way."
  • The idea is partly personal: her mother is hard of hearing, which got Tuteja thinking about workplace barriers. Job postings describe what employers expect, she noticed, but rarely what the day-to-day experience actually feels like — the gap Raaha's quiz tries to close.
  • Both tools are free and built for accessibility: Raaha for job seekers, and Legible, her other project, which simplifies special-education documents like IEPs and 504 plans for families. She also runs Empower InvisAbilities, a student-led nonprofit raising awareness of neurodiversity and invisible disabilities.

The news

A 17-year-old who can't open ChatGPT on her school's Wi-Fi has built an AI startup with more than a thousand users. Navya Tuteja, a senior at Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology in Virginia, launched Raaha two months ago — a free, AI-powered platform that lets neurodivergent job seekers assess whether a job listing is a suitable fit before they invest hours in an application.

Raaha runs listings through a quiz-based system that scores them across several factors, giving candidates a realistic read on the potential workplace and day-to-day experience rather than just the employer's requirements. The platform already covers more than 20,000 listings, Fortune reported.

"It made me use it in school way less. So I guess, as annoying as it was, it was still good, in a way."

— Navya Tuteja, on her school's AI restrictions, to Fortune

Context & background

Tuteja's route into AI entrepreneurship runs straight through the restriction meant to keep her away from it. Thomas Jefferson blocks ChatGPT, Claude and similar tools on its network, forcing her to do schoolwork and exam preparation independently. Rather than resenting the ban, she credits it with teaching her when AI is useful and when it should be left aside — she uses it for drafting emails and organising information, but not for material she needs to learn.

That discipline shaped how she built Raaha: she wrote the underlying algorithm herself and used AI mainly for mechanical aspects like parts of the website's design. She has argued that young founders should be transparent about how they use AI — a stance her parents, Deepti and Rohit Tuteja, reinforced at home: AI can assist her work, but the thinking must remain her own.

Bootstrapped and free for now, Raaha may later charge employers and workforce organisations; Tuteja plans to attend college but would consider running it full-time if growth continues.

Impact & analysis

Raaha sits at the intersection of two live debates: how schools should handle generative AI, and how hiring fails neurodivergent candidates. On the first, Tuteja is a case study for regulation over prohibition — a student who learned the technology's limits precisely because she couldn't lean on it. On the second, she spotted a genuine market failure: job ads are written entirely from the employer's side, and candidates who need to know about sensory environments or communication norms get nothing.

Her work extends beyond Raaha. Legible, her tool for simplifying IEPs and 504 plans, grew from the observation that AI summaries can make it harder for parents to trace claims to original sources — leading her to propose a transparency standard she calls Traceable Accessibility, which she has discussed with state lawmakers and the US Department of Education.

"I don't think banning it is the solution. I think you have to regulate it in the right way."

— Navya Tuteja, on generative AI in schools

The diaspora angle

Tuteja's story is a diaspora arc with a twist: the ambition points outward — at accessibility and lawmakers — and her mother's experience with hearing loss, not a coding competition, was the founding insight. She is already lobbying on AI governance before she can vote.

What's next

For now, Raaha stays free and her college plans hold. The open questions: will employers pay to be scored, and will her Traceable Accessibility standard gain traction with regulators? Either way, a teenager who built an accessibility startup under an AI ban has made her point — the issue is whether anyone teaches young people to use AI thoughtfully.
nri_angle: Navya Tuteja, an Indian-origin teen, is already lobbying state lawmakers and the US Department of Education on AI transparency — a sign of Indian-American youth moving from tech achievement into tech policymaking.
author: Diaspora Desk
